analysis.one_liner: Cuts all funding for the federal workplace safety agency to zero for one year.
analysis.headline: Six House Republicans sponsored the bill to cut OSHA's funding to zero, and it died in committee without a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This one-page bill would bar any federal money from going to the Occupational Safety and Health Administration for fiscal year 2024 — effectively shutting it down. OSHA is the agency that inspects workplaces, sets safety standards like fall protection and limits on toxic exposure, and fines employers when workers are hurt or killed on the job. Zeroing out its budget would end inspections, enforcement, and fines for a year. The bill never moved past its referral to the House Education and Workforce Committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Employers, particularly those with unsafe conditions or pending OSHA citations, would gain a year with no inspections, no new standards, and no fines. Businesses that spend money on compliance — safety equipment, training, recordkeeping — would also save those costs.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Employers facing safety inspections and fines

how_it_helps.text: The bill sets a ceiling of $0 on all funds authorized or made available to OSHA for fiscal year 2024, regardless of any other law.
With no funding, OSHA could not carry out inspections, issue standards, or enforce workplace safety rules during that year.

analysis.who_pays: Workers. OSHA's inspections and enforcement are the main federal check on unsafe workplaces; without them, hazards go unexamined and violations carry no penalty. Injured workers and their families also lose the ability to rely on federal enforcement when safety rules are broken.

drawbacks.text: The only direct benefit of the bill is reduced federal spending; it saves no money for workers and would leave workplaces without any federal safety enforcement for a year.

An honest supporter would have to acknowledge that eliminating OSHA's budget suspends the entire federal framework of workplace safety standards — not just spending on paperwork, but the inspections and penalties that give the standards force.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The trade is lopsided against the public. The gain is modest federal savings; the loss is a full year of workplace inspections, safety standard-setting, and enforcement covering most American workplaces. The bill made no attempt to trim the agency or narrow its authority — it defunded it entirely.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Education and Workforce Committee in March 2023 and the committee never took it up before Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Andy Biggs introduced the bill on March 29, 2023, with five Republican cosponsors: Reps. Rosendale, Gaetz, Good of Virginia, Roy, and Crane.
The House referred it to the Committee on Education and the Workforce the same day.
No further action — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — appears in the bill's action history through the end of the 118th Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The public is better off because it died: workers kept a funded OSHA. The employers the bill would have shielded from inspections and fines did not get that shield.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Workers; the bill never got a hearing

for.name: Rep. Andy Biggs
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to zero out OSHA's fiscal year 2024 funding.

against.name: House Committee on Education and the Workforce
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a hearing, markup, or vote; the bill sat after referral until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: All six supporters were Republicans; no Democrat sponsored or cosponsored the bill, and it drew only 5 cosponsors out of 224 House Republicans [S4].

industries.note: Zeroing out OSHA's budget would have freed employers from federal inspections, citations, and fines for a year. The gain to employers would come directly at workers' expense, since enforcement is what makes safety standards real.
